query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic face-centered-cubic high-entropy alloys (HEAs), lattice distortion strength—quantified by the atomic size mismatch parameter δ—governs hardness and yield strength by impeding dislocation motion via solid‐solution strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast or homogenized, single‐phase equiatomic fcc HEAs with controlled grain size (~20 µm), identical chemistry except for systematic variation of atomic radii spread.
generation.intervention: Prepare a series of five equiatomic fcc HEAs (five elements each) in which δ is varied from ~1% to ~6% by replacing one element with successively larger or smaller atoms, while holding valence electron concentration, processing, and grain size constant.
generation.conditions: Room temperature mechanical testing; annealed to eliminate residual stresses; same cold-work history; oxygen content <100 ppm.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion (δ) measured via X-ray diffraction peak broadening and atomic pair distribution function analysis.
generation.mechanism: Increasing δ raises the local stress field heterogeneity around solute atoms, increasing the critical resolved shear stress needed for dislocation glide, thereby strengthening the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Hardness (by nanoindentation) and 0.2% yield strength (by micro-tensile tests) increase approximately linearly with δ, e.g. yield strength rising ~50–80 MPa per 1% δ increase up to ~6% δ.
generation.baseline: An equiatomic fcc HEA with δ≈3% shows ~3 GPa hardness and ~500 MPa yield strength.
generation.boundary: Effect holds for single‐phase fcc HEAs with δ between ~1% and ~6%; beyond ~6%, intermetallic phases or excessive short‐range order may form and invalidate the linear trend.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of strengthening per δ unit may vary ±20% due to residual microsegregation or minor stacking‐fault energy differences; phase stability must be confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two HEAs with identical δ (~4%) but differing in another parameter (e.g., valence electron concentration or grain size) held nominally equal in the primary series. Test hardness and yield strength under identical conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with equal δ but different secondary parameters produce significantly different hardness or strength (>10% deviation), then lattice distortion alone does not govern strengthening, falsifying the hypothesis.
